topic.ru: Три текста: муравьи-земледельцы и их грибные сады, как картофель завоевал Европу и спор о том, стоит ли спасать исчезающие языки.

textTitles: The tuber that fed a continent
Is it worth saving a dying language?

paragraphs.text: Agriculture is usually described as a human invention, dating back some twelve thousand years. It is not. Several groups of insects began cultivating food tens of millions of years earlier, and the most sophisticated of them, the leafcutter ants of the American tropics, run operations that bear comparison with human farms in their division of labour, their management of pests and their dependence on a single crop. Studying them has become a way of asking which features of agriculture are general solutions to the problem of growing food and which are peculiar to our own species. The answer matters beyond biology, because the problems the ants face are ones that human farmers have not always solved.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The crop is a fungus, and the ants do not eat the leaves they are famous for carrying. Workers cut fragments of fresh vegetation, carry them back to the nest and hand them to smaller workers, who chew them into a pulp and use it as a growing medium for the fungus. The fungus in turn produces swollen tips rich in nutrients, which the ants harvest and feed to their larvae. The relationship is so close that neither partner can live without the other: the fungus is not found growing wild, and the ants cannot digest the leaves themselves.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: A mature colony is an industrial enterprise. It may contain several million workers, occupy an underground nest with hundreds of chambers, and strip a quantity of vegetation in a year that rivals the appetite of a large grazing mammal. The labour is divided by size, which varies enormously within a single colony: the largest workers defend the nest and clear foraging trails, medium-sized workers cut and carry leaves, and the smallest tend the fungus in the chambers and ride on the leaf fragments being carried home, where they appear to protect the carriers from parasitic flies. The nest itself is ventilated by a system of tunnels that draws fresh air through the fungus chambers, keeping carbon dioxide and humidity within limits the crop can tolerate.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Like human farmers, the ants face disease. Their gardens are threatened by a specialised mould that can overrun the fungus and destroy a colony’s food supply within days. The ants respond in several ways. Workers inspect the gardens constantly and remove infected material, which is carried to dedicated waste chambers tended by older ants that do not return to the gardens. They also carry on their bodies colonies of bacteria that produce substances which suppress the mould, a partnership that researchers compare to the use of pesticides, though with the important difference that the ants’ defences appear to have remained effective for millions of years.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: That durability is the most striking contrast with human agriculture. Human farmers who rely on a single variety of a crop grown in large quantities have repeatedly suffered sudden losses when a disease adapted to it, and the pesticides used to protect crops lose effectiveness as pests evolve resistance. The ants also rely on a narrow range of fungal varieties, yet their gardens have not collapsed in the same way. One explanation is that the bacteria they carry are themselves evolving, so that the defence changes alongside the threat; another is that the ants combine several methods at once, so that no single weakness is fatal.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The history of ant agriculture has been reconstructed by comparing the genes of living species. The earliest fungus-growing ants, which appeared around sixty million years ago, collected dead plant material and insect droppings rather than fresh leaves, and grew fungi that could also survive outside the nest. Cutting living leaves appeared much later, perhaps in the last fifteen to twenty million years, and coincided with the fungus becoming fully dependent on its growers. The transition appears to have occurred in dry habitats, where the ants may have kept their crop alive by protecting it from conditions it could not tolerate alone. The oldest lineages still survive alongside the leafcutters.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The comparison with human farming can be pushed too far. Ants did not choose to farm; the behaviour evolved through natural selection over millions of generations, whereas human agriculture was developed, spread and modified within a few thousand years by people who could observe results and change their methods. Nor do the ants trade, store surplus in the human sense, or build anything resembling the social hierarchy that followed the first human harvests. What the parallels show is that certain problems, such as disease in a crop grown at high density, arise whenever food is produced in this way, not that insects and people solve them by the same means. The resemblance is one of problems rather than of minds.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Some researchers nonetheless believe that the ants have something practical to teach. The bacteria they carry have been examined as sources of new antibiotic compounds, and several substances with promising properties have been identified. More broadly, the success of a system that has resisted disease for millions of years has encouraged interest in agricultural methods that use several defences together rather than relying on a single chemical. Whether those lessons transfer to human farms remains to be tested, but the ants have had a long time to get it right. Few human farming systems can claim anything similar.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: The tuber that fed a continent

paragraphs.text: The potato arrived in Europe in the second half of the sixteenth century, carried from the Andes, where it had been cultivated for thousands of years and where farmers grew hundreds of varieties adapted to different altitudes. For roughly two centuries after its arrival it remained a curiosity in most of the continent, grown in botanical gardens, fed to animals or eaten by the poor in a few regions. Its eventual adoption as a staple food was neither quick nor inevitable, and the reasons it took so long reveal as much about European society as about the plant itself. The Spanish, who first brought it across the Atlantic, did not at first regard it as a food for themselves at all.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Part of the problem was botanical. The first potatoes brought to Europe came from regions near the equator, where the length of the day varies little through the year, and they were adapted to form tubers only when days were short. In the long summer days of northern Europe they produced leaves and flowers but few tubers until late in the autumn, when frost often destroyed the plants first. Only after varieties from further south in South America, adapted to longer days, were introduced or selected did the potato become a reliable crop in northern latitudes. The problem was solved by selection rather than by any deliberate programme of breeding, and it took generations.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Suspicion also played a part, although its importance is often exaggerated in popular accounts. The potato belongs to a family of plants that includes several poisonous species, and its green parts are indeed toxic; it grew underground, unlike the grains that formed the basis of the European diet; and it was unfamiliar in a way that made cooks and consumers wary. Historians now argue that such objections were real but secondary, and that farmers were mainly reluctant to change the crop rotations and customs around which village life, taxation and the rights to common land were organised. Rules governing which crops could be planted in which fields were often fixed by custom, and a farmer who departed from them risked disputes with his neighbours.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: When the potato did spread, it did so for practical reasons. An acre of potatoes could feed several times as many people as an acre of grain, the crop could be grown on small plots and poor soil, and because the tubers stayed in the ground until needed they were less vulnerable than stored grain to armies requisitioning supplies. Governments in several countries promoted it during the eighteenth century, distributing seed potatoes and publishing instructions, particularly after harvest failures had shown how exposed a population dependent on a single grain could be. Some rulers are said to have planted the crop in guarded fields to make it look valuable, though several of these stories are probably later inventions.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The consequences for population were considerable. Economic historians have estimated that the introduction of the potato may account for around a quarter of the growth in population and urbanisation in the Old World between the late seventeenth and late nineteenth centuries. The calculation rests on comparing regions whose soil and climate suited the crop with those where it grew poorly, and it is not universally accepted, but the direction of the effect is not seriously disputed: more food from the same land allowed more people to survive childhood, and many of them eventually moved to the growing industrial towns.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Dependence brought its own danger. In regions where the poor came to rely on the potato for almost all their food, often grown from a very small number of varieties, a single disease could destroy the harvest across an entire country. When a mould that attacks potato plants arrived in Europe in the 1840s, it spread rapidly through crops that had little genetic variety to resist it. The resulting famines led to widespread hunger and emigration, and they became the most frequently cited example of the risks of relying on a narrow genetic base, a lesson repeated in agricultural textbooks ever since.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The Andean farmers had avoided that danger, not by accident but by method. In a single field they planted many varieties with different tastes, colours and resistances, so that no single disease or frost could destroy the whole harvest. Much of that diversity is still maintained by farming communities in the region, and scientists breeding potatoes for resistance to disease or drought now regularly return to it. A collection of thousands of traditional varieties is kept in a gene bank in the Andes, and material from it has been used in breeding programmes around the world.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The potato is now among the most widely grown food crops in the world, and most of its production takes place outside both the continent where it originated and the continent that adopted it so slowly. Its history is often told as a story of European ingenuity overcoming prejudice, but a fairer summary is that it spread when the circumstances made it useful, flourished while those circumstances lasted, and exposed the costs of uniformity in a way that its original growers had understood for centuries. Few crops illustrate so clearly how much the success of a plant depends on the society that receives it.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Is it worth saving a dying language?

paragraphs.text: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, a large proportion are used by fewer than ten thousand people, and many are no longer being learned by children. Linguists estimate that, without intervention, a substantial share of them will have no speakers by the end of the century. Efforts to reverse this decline, usually described as language revitalisation, have multiplied in recent decades, supported by communities, universities and in some cases governments. Whether such efforts are worthwhile, and what counts as success, are questions on which people who care about languages disagree more than outsiders might expect. The disagreements are not only academic, since they determine how scarce money and the time of elderly speakers are used.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Kiri Walker, who has worked with several revitalisation programmes, argues that the most important measure is whether children acquire the language at home. Documentation, dictionaries and adult classes are valuable, she says, but a language survives only when parents use it with their children as a matter of course. The programmes she regards as most successful began with immersion nurseries, where young children spent the day with fluent elderly speakers, and then extended the same approach into primary schools. In her experience the parents who sent their children to these nurseries often began learning the language themselves, so that the effort spread upwards through the family.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Leonid Petrov, a linguist, places greater value on recording. Many languages have features found nowhere else, ways of expressing direction, time or evidence that tell researchers something about the range of what human languages can do, and when a language disappears without being documented that knowledge is lost permanently. He does not oppose revitalisation but warns that it sometimes absorbs the time of the last fluent speakers in teaching basic vocabulary, when they could be recording the complex grammar and specialised knowledge that only they possess. In his view, a thorough record should be the first priority, since it is also the foundation for any later attempt to teach the language.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The economic argument is made most often by those who question revitalisation. Speakers of a small language, they point out, frequently need a larger language for education and employment, and parents who choose to raise their children in the dominant language are usually making a rational decision about their children’s prospects rather than rejecting their heritage. Nadia Farouk, who studies language policy, takes this argument seriously but notes that bilingualism is the normal condition for most of the world’s population, and that learning a heritage language has not been shown to harm children’s performance in the dominant one. The choice, she suggests, is rarely as stark as it is presented.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The rights of speakers are a further consideration. In many places the decline of a language was not the result of free choice but of policies that punished children for speaking it at school or excluded the language from public life. For communities with that history, revitalisation is less a matter of preserving linguistic diversity than of repairing a damage deliberately done, and Farouk argues that outsiders who question the cost of such programmes should remember that the original loss was also produced by public policy. Several governments have since apologised for such policies and now fund teaching in the languages concerned.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Technology has changed what is possible, though less than was once hoped. Recordings, online dictionaries and learning applications have made materials available to scattered communities and to young people who might never attend a class. Tomás Ibarra, who designs language-learning software for small communities, cautions that an application cannot replace a speaking community: learners who study alone rarely progress beyond basic phrases, and the programmes he considers effective use technology to connect learners with each other and with speakers rather than as a substitute for them. Software, in his words, is a meeting place rather than a teacher.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Success is difficult to define. Very few languages that had lost all their child speakers have returned to everyday use across a whole community, and the best-known case is often treated as an exception that others cannot easily repeat. Yet many programmes that have not produced large numbers of fluent speakers have nonetheless increased the number of people who can use the language in ceremonies, songs and greetings, and communities often regard this as a worthwhile result in itself. Judging such efforts only by the number of native speakers produced may miss much of what they are for. The size of a community also matters: a language with a few hundred speakers faces different choices from one with tens of thousands.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The question in the title therefore has more than one answer, depending on what the language is being saved for. If the aim is scientific knowledge, documentation matters most; if it is a living community of speakers, the home and the nursery matter most; and if it is the repair of a historical injustice, the decision properly belongs to the community itself. What seems clear is that the choice should be made deliberately and early, because each of these aims becomes much harder to achieve once the last fluent speakers are gone. Waiting for certainty, in this field, is itself a decision.
paragraphs.label: H
